title: Journal of Experimental Psychology: General - Vol 155, Iss 11

items.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
items.content: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these “strength-based organizational approaches” and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees’ broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants’ likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees’ equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees’ lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors’ positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person–context interactions. items.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
items.content: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens (“in” or “on”) but rather as objects’ properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
items.content: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. items.title: The orthographic mind: Orthographic imagery propensity correlates with semantic structure and sensory sensitivity.
items.content: Individuals differ in their habitual use of internal representational modes, including visual imagery, internal verbalization, and orthographic imagery (the mental simulation of written word forms). The present research examined whether such internal representational propensities relate to semantic organization and external information engagement. Across two studies (total N = 1,399), we assessed individuals’ internal representational modes using the Internal Representations Questionnaire and examined their associations with semantic structure (nine-word semantic rating experiments; N = 1,109) and external information engagement (sensory-processing sensitivity and mobile app usage). Orthographic imagery showed robust associations with both semantic geometry and external information engagement patterns: Individuals with stronger orthographic imagery showed greater cross-category semantic association strength, lower semantic conformity, and lower sensory-processing sensitivity. Internal verbalization was positively associated with within-category semantic cohesion, while visual imagery showed no reliable associations with semantic geometry and limited associations with real-world media engagement. Effects were modest but consistent across experiments. These findings suggest that internal representational modes function as stable weighting biases, subtly modulating semantic geometry and sensory-processing profiles. Such propensities therefore correspond to structured variations in cognition, rather than merely phenomenological differences in inner experience. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
items.content: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5–6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5–6 and 8–9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor’s color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5–6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. items.title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices.
items.content: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in “master virtues” that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a “master virtue.” However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful “master vices.” These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people’s beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. items.title: Enacted love: Capitalization responses signal love, including toward strangers.
items.content: What behavior is seen as “love” and why does it matter? We theorize active-constructive responding to another’s disclosure of good news is prototypical “enacted love” and test hypotheses about implications for a loving person’s relationship development. We use three distinct methods—dyadic interactions between romantic couples (Study 1, N = 160), real spontaneous responses to a stranger’s good news (Study 2, N = 204), and observation of others’ real capitalization responses to a stranger’s good news (Studies 3–5, N = 97, 105, and 402, respectively)—to assess convergent and discriminant evidence for the construct. Study 2 uses experience sampling to track the development of capitalization respondents’ social lives over time. Studies 4 and 5 use within-subjects experiments to test hypotheses that loving behavior could influence others’ interactions with loving people. Results have theoretical implications for close relationships and the concept of “loving one’s neighbor,” plus practical implications for building bridges in a divided society. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
items.content: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people’s memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition—a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative—but not item—memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges.
